readings.title: The Trumpet
readings.challenge: Hear how a call to rise turns from dreams and lovers toward “the old wars.”
readings.focus: A dawn summons that praises the earth and sends men to war in the same breath.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. He wrote this poem in 1916, while training as an artillery officer; in army camps a trumpet sounded reveille, the morning call to rise.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE TRUMPET; opens “RISE up, rise up, And, as the trumpet blowing Chases the dreams of men, As the dawn…”; closes “…the stars Through all the dewy night: Up with the light, To the old wars; Arise, arise!”.

questions.prompt: What does the trumpet chase away in the first stanza, and what are the listeners told to scatter?
facilitatorNotes: The dreams of men, as dawn chases the stars; then the dew that covers “the print of last night’s lovers.” The call erases the traces of private night and love.
evidence: Chases the dreams of men,
The print of last night's lovers--

questions.prompt: “Forget, men, everything . . . / Except that it is lovelier / Than any mysteries.” What should the listeners remember, and why might soldiers need to?
facilitatorNotes: The newborn earth’s beauty, which outshines any mystery (religious, dreamed or hidden). It is the one thing worth carrying into the day, a reason for living that asks no explanation.
evidence: Except that it is lovelier
Than any mysteries.

questions.prompt: The poem ends “Up with the light, / To the old wars; / Arise, arise!” Is the ending rousing, ironic, or both? Use earlier images.
facilitatorNotes: The quick rhythm and the dawn are exhilarating, but “old” wars suggests endless repetition, and the lovers’ traces have just been scattered. Written by a soldier who would die in battle, it can be heard as eager, as grimly resigned, or as both at once.
evidence: To the old wars;
Open your eyes to the air

readings.title: Two Pewits
readings.challenge: Track the opposites (white and black, earth and sky, cry and silence) and find where the speaker places himself.
readings.focus: Birds that refuse to choose between earth and sky, watched by a “ghost.”
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Pewits, also called lapwings, are black-and-white birds of open fields, known for their wild tumbling flight and plaintive cry.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem TWO PEWITS; opens “UNDER the after-sunset sky Two pewits sport and cry, More white than is the moon on high…”; closes “…earth and sky, While the moon's quarter silently Rides, and earth rests as silently.”.

questions.prompt: How can the pewits be “More white than is the moon” and “More black than earth”?
facilitatorNotes: Their plumage is both; in the half-light one side flashes white and the other shows dark as they turn. They seem to belong to sky and earth at once.
evidence: More white than is the moon on high
More black than earth.

questions.prompt: Almost every line ends on the same sound as “sky” and “cry.” What does this repeated rhyme do, and what changes in the last lines?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme returns like the birds’ insistent call and their up-and-down flight. The last two lines shift to “silently,” and the poem closes in the moon’s and the earth’s quiet.
evidence: Is the one sound under the sky.
Rides, and earth rests as silently.

questions.prompt: Who is “the ghost who wonders why”? Why might the speaker see himself that way?
facilitatorNotes: The human watcher, silent in the dusk, outside the birds’ merriment. A ghost belongs neither to earth nor sky; unlike the birds, he cannot enjoy both. Some read melancholy, others a wry, self-mocking aside.
evidence: Over the ghost who wonders why
Nor choose 'twixt earth and sky,

readings.title: Swedes
readings.challenge: Follow a comparison that sets a farmyard heap beside a Pharaoh’s tomb, and decide which the poem prefers.
readings.focus: Ordinary winter food revealed as a kind of treasure.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Swedes (rutabagas) were stored through winter in a long pile covered with earth; here workers have opened it. Archaeologists had recently opened royal tombs in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings; Amen-hotep is a pharaoh’s name.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem SWEDES; opens “THEY have taken the gable from the roof of clay On the long swede pile. They have let in…”; closes “But dreamless long-dead Amen-hotep lies. This is a dream of Winter, sweet as Spring.”.

questions.prompt: What has been uncovered at the start, and what colours does it reveal?
facilitatorNotes: The earth “gable” of the swede pile has been taken off, letting sun onto pale shoots that grew in the dark: white, gold and purple.
evidence: THEY have taken the gable from the roof of clay
To the white and gold and purple of curled fronds

questions.prompt: Why compare this to a boy crawling into a Pharaoh’s tomb? What does the boy see?
facilitatorNotes: Mummy, gods, chariot, throne, pottery, alabaster, gold: the splendour of the dead. The swede pile is “more tender-gorgeous”: tender because alive and humble, gorgeous in colour.
evidence: It is a sight more tender-gorgeous
A boy crawls down into a Pharaoh's tomb

questions.prompt: “But dreamless long-dead Amen-hotep lies. / This is a dream of Winter, sweet as Spring.” What distinction do the last two lines make?
facilitatorNotes: The pharaoh’s treasure surrounds a corpse without dreams; the sprouting swedes are winter dreaming of spring, life kept in darkness. Some read a preference for humble living things over imperial grandeur; others note that “dream” can also mean illusion.
evidence: But dreamless long-dead Amen-hotep lies.
This is a dream of Winter, sweet as Spring.

readings.title: Like the Touch of Rain
readings.challenge: Follow a simile through the whole poem and find where it breaks.
readings.focus: A remembered parting turned into a door shut against the rain.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. The poem is a brief memory of a woman and two words she said.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem LIKE THE TOUCH OF RAIN; opens “LIKE the touch of rain she was On a man's flesh and hair and eyes When the joy of walking…”; closes “…door Between me and the blessed rain That was never shut before And will not open again.”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening simile compare “she” to, and what kind of man feels it?
facilitatorNotes: The touch of rain on a man who has been surprised by joy while walking: sudden, fresh, exhilarating.
evidence: LIKE the touch of rain she was
When the joy of walking thus

questions.prompt: How is the walker of the second stanza different from the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: The walker loves the storm and then forgets it when he gets home; the speaker will not forget “Go now.” The general case becomes painfully personal.
evidence: But forgets when he returns
As I shall not forget her "Go now."

questions.prompt: “Those two words shut a door / Between me and the blessed rain.” What has been lost: the woman, or something larger?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps the woman; perhaps the power to feel joy as the rain once gave it. A door “never shut before” that “will not open again” suggests a permanent change in the speaker. Readers can argue for either, or both.
evidence: Those two words shut a door
That was never shut before

readings.title: If I Should Ever by Chance
readings.challenge: Work out the terms of an imaginary lease, and the joke hidden in its last condition.
readings.focus: A father’s gift that costs nothing and asks for close attention to the world.
readings.context: One of four “household poems” Thomas wrote in 1916 for his family, while he was a soldier teaching map-reading at an army camp in Essex; most of the names are farms and hamlets near that camp. This one is for his elder daughter, Bronwen. To let is to rent out; orchises are wild orchids; furze (gorse) is a prickly shrub that flowers in almost every month of the year.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem IF I SHOULD EVER BY CHANCE; opens “IF I should ever by chance grow rich I'll buy Codham, Cockridden, and Childerditch,…”; closes “…Childerditch, Roses, Pyrgo and Lapwater,-- I shall give them all to my elder daughter.”.

questions.prompt: What “rent” will the elder daughter pay, and what does it show about what her father values?
facilitatorNotes: Each year’s first violets, primroses and orchises, found before he finds them: attention and delight in the countryside, not money.
evidence: Each year's first violets, white and lonely,
She must find them before I do, that is.

questions.prompt: Why does the furze matter, given that it blooms almost all year?
facilitatorNotes: If she finds a blossom on furze, the lands are hers forever, and she nearly always can: the condition is a loving loophole, a joke that makes the gift permanent.
evidence: But if she finds a blossom on furze
Without rent they shall all for ever be hers,

questions.prompt: The poem begins “If I should ever by chance grow rich.” How does that “if” shape the gift, and what does it suggest about the father’s real situation?
facilitatorNotes: He is not rich and will not own these farms; the gift is imaginary. Yet the names, said twice, are a real gift: the music of the places themselves. Given that he was a soldier when he wrote it, readers may find it playful, poignant, or both.
evidence: IF I should ever by chance grow rich
I shall give them all to my elder daughter.

readings.title: What Shall I Give?
readings.challenge: Follow a list of things a father will not give, and find what he gives instead.
readings.focus: Wealth refused as a burden; a child left her own small world.
readings.context: One of four “household poems” Thomas wrote in 1916 for his family, while he was a soldier teaching map-reading at an army camp in Essex; most of the names are farms and hamlets near that camp. This one is for his younger daughter, Myfanwy. Havering-atte-Bower in Essex was once a royal palace; Samarcand is a fabled city of Central Asia; the Pleiades are a cluster of stars; Steep is the Hampshire village where the family lived; to cumber is to burden.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem WHAT SHALL I GIVE?; opens “WHAT shall I give my daughter the younger More than will keep her from cold and hunger? I…”; closes “…hair uncurled, Wanting a thousand little things That time without contentment brings.”.

questions.prompt: What does the father decide to give, and why does he refuse acres and brooks?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing beyond what keeps her from cold and hunger. Land would make her no richer, only burdened; he calls acres “lumber.”
evidence: I shall not give her anything.
Her small hands I would not cumber

questions.prompt: What does the queen in Havering Bower suggest about wealth and power?
facilitatorNotes: She had pleasure and power but sat “Alone, with the shadows”: possession brings no company and no happiness.
evidence: She would be no richer than the queen
Alone, with the shadows, pleasure and power.

questions.prompt: The poem ends with the child “Wanting a thousand little things / That time without contentment brings.” Is wanting a gift? Explain.
facilitatorNotes: He leaves her Steep, her own world, her “spectacled self,” and the desires of growing up. Wanting keeps a life moving and keeps her herself. But “without contentment” may also mean restlessness; readers can hear wisdom, sadness, or both.
evidence: But leave her Steep and her own world
Wanting a thousand little things

readings.title: If I Were to Own
readings.challenge: Work out an imagined bargain between father and son, and notice the turn when the father pictures himself old.
readings.focus: Land traded for a blackbird’s song, and a father’s fear of destroying it.
readings.context: One of four “household poems” Thomas wrote in 1916 for his family, while he was a soldier teaching map-reading at an army camp in Essex; most of the names are farms and hamlets near that camp. This one is for his son, Merfyn. A tye is an Essex word for a green or common; plovers are lapwings; “for a song” also means very cheaply.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem IF I WERE TO OWN; opens “IF I were to own this countryside As far as a man in a day could ride, And the Tyes were…”; closes “…Martins, Lambkins, or Lillyputs, Should be his till the cart tracks had no ruts.”.

questions.prompt: What rent would the father ask his son for each place?
facilitatorNotes: A blackbird’s song at dawn: one song for the use of any of the farms. The phrase “for a song” means almost nothing, and here means something precious.
evidence: For a song, a blackbird's song, at dawn.
If he would let me any one

questions.prompt: Explain the strange situation in which the father ends “old and alone.”
facilitatorNotes: If he had shot every blackbird to put in a pie, he would have no songs left to pay with, so the son would have everything and the father nothing. Destroying beauty for appetite costs him his place.
evidence: Had shot them to put them into a pie,--
And I was left old and alone.

questions.prompt: Why list so many place names, twice? What do the names do in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Their sounds are a pleasure in themselves, and reciting them is a way of possessing places without owning them. The names are the real gift to the boy. The last line promises them to him for as long as the cart tracks last.
evidence: Shellow, Rochetts, Bandish, and Pickerells,
Should be his till the cart tracks had no ruts.

readings.title: And You, Helen
readings.challenge: Notice which gifts are things and which are qualities, and what the last gift admits.
readings.focus: A husband’s gifts that confess what he has cost his wife.
readings.context: One of four “household poems” Thomas wrote in 1916 for his family, while he was a soldier teaching map-reading at an army camp in Essex; most of the names are farms and hamlets near that camp. This one, the last, is for his wife, Helen Thomas.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem AND YOU, HELEN; opens “AND you, Helen, what should I give you? So many things I would give you Had I an infinite…”; closes “…foul and fair, And myself, too, if I could find Where it lay hidden and it proved kind.”.

questions.prompt: List what the speaker would give Helen from “an infinite great store.” Which are things and which are qualities?
facilitatorNotes: Lands, waters, flowers, wine are things; youth, loveliness, truth, a clear eye, a better art, children as many as she wished are qualities or chances. Most of the gifts cannot be bought.
evidence: So many things I would give you
Lands, waters, flowers, wine,

questions.prompt: “I would give you back yourself.” What does this suggest Helen has lost, and to whom?
facilitatorNotes: “All you have lost . . . Or given to me”: some of herself went into the marriage and to him. The line quietly admits a cost he caused.
evidence: I would give you back yourself,
Or given to me.

questions.prompt: The final gift is “myself, too, if I could find / Where it lay hidden and it proved kind.” What does this admit about the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: He does not know where his own self is, or whether it would be kind if found: an honest confession of withdrawal and difficulty. Readers may find it bleak, loving, or both at once.
evidence: And myself, too, if I could find
Where it lay hidden and it proved kind.

readings.title: When First
readings.challenge: Follow sentences that run across stanza breaks, and find the one thing the speaker says has gone for ever.
readings.focus: Hope distinguished from health and cheerfulness, and love that grows with use.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. The speaker walks for the last time down a chalk hill he has known for twelve years.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem WHEN FIRST; opens “WHEN first I came here I had hope, Hope for I knew not what. Fast beat My heart at sight…”; closes “…time and necessity Will grow, and louder the heart's dance At parting than at meeting be.”.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker feel when he first came here?
facilitatorNotes: Hope “for I knew not what”: his heart beat at the sight of the slope, as if climbing it would show him something no other hill could.
evidence: Hope for I knew not what.
Would see something no other hill

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker separate hope from “health” and “cheerfulness”?
facilitatorNotes: Health and cheerfulness come and go within an hour; hope, once gone, does not return. The careful distinction makes the loss exact rather than general gloom.
evidence: Hope now,--not health, nor cheerfulness,
Just hope has gone for ever.

questions.prompt: The last stanza says love grows with “chance / And use and time and necessity,” and the heart dances louder at parting. Is this a consolation, and how does it change what came before?
facilitatorNotes: Love has taken hope’s place: what grows from long familiarity is stronger, at the moment of leaving, than the first excitement was. Some readers find comfort; others a sad paradox that we know love best when we lose it. Notice how the run-on stanzas carry the thought forward like a walk downhill.
evidence: One thing I know, that love with chance
At parting than at meeting be.

readings.title: Fifty Faggots
readings.challenge: Notice how a stack of firewood leads the speaker to think about time and the war.
readings.focus: What a bird takes for permanent, and what a man cannot foresee.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Faggots are bundles of sticks cut from underwood (young hazel and ash) for firewood; a copse is a small wood. The poem was written in 1916.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem FIFTY FAGGOTS; opens “THERE they stand, on their ends, the fifty faggots That once were underwood of hazel and…”; closes “…things Have ended, maybe, that I can no more Foresee or more control than robin and wren.”.

questions.prompt: What will the faggots become for the birds next spring, and why not this spring?
facilitatorNotes: A thicket for a blackbird or robin to nest in, trusted because to a bird whatever exists lasts forever. This spring it is too late: the swifts have arrived and nesting has begun.
evidence: Whatever is for ever to a bird:
This Spring it is too late; the swift has come.

questions.prompt: “Better they will never warm me.” Why might the speaker say this?
facilitatorNotes: On the surface he complains of carrying them on a hot day; underneath, he may not be there to burn them, since the fires will last several winters and the war goes on. The joke carries a foreboding.
evidence: Better they will never warm me, though they must
Light several Winters' fires.

questions.prompt: How does the ending put the speaker on a level with the robin and the wren? Is that comforting?
facilitatorNotes: He can no more foresee or control what will end, including perhaps his own life, than the birds can. The calm, plain tone holds the fear steady. Some readers find acceptance here, others a quiet dread.
evidence: The war will have ended, many other things
Foresee or more control than robin and wren.

readings.title: Women He Liked
readings.challenge: Follow how a man and the lane named after him are remembered, and what the name keeps and loses.
readings.focus: Naming, memory, and the unintended results of love.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A cob is a sturdy, short-legged horse; the stormcock is the mistle thrush; a slough is a muddy hollow.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem WOMEN HE LIKED; opens “WOMEN he liked, did shovel-bearded Bob, Old Farmer Hayward of the Heath, but he Loved…”; closes “…the elms have turned the lane to slough And gloom, the name alone survives, Bob's Lane.”.

questions.prompt: What did Bob Hayward love most, and what did that love lead him to do?
facilitatorNotes: Women he liked, horses he loved, but trees most of all; he planted elms all along the lane.
evidence: Loved horses.
He planted elms where now the stormcock sings

questions.prompt: “To name a thing beloved man sometimes fails.” What does this line mean in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The track was lovely, with thickets and nightingales, yet no one had named it; people often fail to name what they love. Bob’s planting gave it a name by accident.
evidence: To name a thing beloved man sometimes fails.
Till then the track had never had a name

questions.prompt: Bob’s elms have turned the lane to mud and gloom, and no one passes now. Is the ending ironic, sad, or both? What survives?
facilitatorNotes: His love for trees ruined the lane he loved; only the name, “Bob’s Lane,” is left. Memory outlasts use, and the man survives in a word rather than a place.
evidence: Out of the elms have turned the lane to slough
And gloom, the name alone survives, Bob's Lane.

readings.title: It Rains
readings.challenge: Hold the speaker’s happiness and sadness together in one scene, and notice what the last image makes of the past.
readings.focus: An empty orchard in the rain, a memory of two walking there, and a flower that seems to hang in the air.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. The “parsley” is cow parsley, a tall wild plant with flat heads of tiny white flowers that grows thick in untended ground. “Fined to naught” means thinned to nothing.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem IT RAINS; opens “IT rains, and nothing stirs within the fence Anywhere through the orchard's untrodden,…”; closes “…Figures, suspended still and ghostly white, The past hovering as it revisits the light.”.

questions.prompt: What details show that no one has been in the orchard?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing stirs; the parsley is “untrodden” and dense as a forest; the raindrops on the grass, “great diamonds,” have no one to break them. The emptiness is made beautiful, not bleak.
evidence: Anywhere through the orchard's untrodden, dense
Of rain on the grassblades there is none to break,

questions.prompt: The speaker is “nearly as happy as possible” and also “Sad.” What makes him happy, what makes him sad, and what does “Unless alone” add?
facilitatorNotes: He is happy to search the wet wilderness and to think of two people walking and kissing there, forgetting the rain; sad that he will never walk so happily in the rain again, “Unless alone.” The two may be himself and someone in the past, or imagined lovers. “Unless alone” can mean solitude is now his only route to that happiness, or that the shared happiness is gone for good; both readings fit.
evidence: And I am nearly as happy as possible
Unless alone, so happy shall I walk

questions.prompt: In the twilight the parsley flower’s stalk disappears and the flower seems to float. How does this image explain “The past hovering as it revisits the light”?
facilitatorNotes: The flower is still there but its support has vanished, so it hangs “suspended still and ghostly white,” as the remembered past returns, vivid but unattached to anything present. “Ghostly” suggests the past is beautiful and also no longer alive.
evidence: Figures, suspended still and ghostly white,
The past hovering as it revisits the light.

readings.title: The Huxter
readings.challenge: Compare what the first stanza lists with what the second stanza adds, and listen to the refrain each time it comes.
readings.focus: A poor, misshapen pedlar who has nothing worth envying, except everything that matters.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A huxter (huckster) is a pedlar who sells small goods from a cart. “A plentiful lack” echoes Hamlet mocking an old man’s “plentiful lack of wit.” Girth is waist size.
readings.contentNote: The huxter’s hunched back is described bluntly, in the period’s manner (“a hump like an ape”).

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE HUXTER; opens “HE has a hump like an ape on his back; He has of money a plentiful lack; And but for a…”; closes “…his lack or his hump; And they laugh as down the lane they bump This fine May morning.”.

questions.prompt: What does the first stanza say the huxter has and lacks? What is the tone of these lines?
facilitatorNotes: A hump, no money, and a gaudy coat twice his size: “not a plainer thing on the earth.” The jingling rhymes and the joke of having “a plentiful lack” sound almost mocking, as if the speaker were sizing him up from outside.
evidence: has a hump like an ape on his back;
He has of money a plentiful lack;

questions.prompt: The second stanza begins with “But.” What does the huxter have after all?
facilitatorNotes: Beer, a cart, and a wife beside him who does not notice his hump or his poverty; they laugh as they bump down the lane. The stanza repeats “lack” and “hump” from the first, but now they are what she does not heed. The list of his deficiencies has become a picture of contentment.
evidence: But the huxter has a bottle of beer;
Who does not heed his lack or his hump;

questions.prompt: “This fine May morning” ends both stanzas. Does it mean the same thing each time?
facilitatorNotes: After the first stanza it sets the plain little man against a fine day; after the second, the fine morning seems to belong to him and his wife as much as to anyone. The refrain stays the same while the reader’s judgment of him changes. Ask what the speaker, a watcher by the lane, may lack that the huxter has.
evidence: This fine May morning.
And they laugh as down the lane they bump

readings.title: A Gentleman
readings.challenge: Hear two speakers judge the same man, and notice the two lines in which the poet judges the first speaker.
readings.focus: Respectable outrage and a poor woman’s loyalty: who decides what makes a gentleman?
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Salisbury, in Wiltshire, held the county courts. The man has robbed gentlemen’s clubs; a lady-killer is a charmer of women. Half a crown was two shillings and sixpence, a crown five shillings: here a payment toward the keep of a baby born out of marriage. A dame is an old woman.
readings.contentNote: An old woman is called a “Gipsy dame,” the period’s term for a Romani traveller; the talk is of theft, a child born out of marriage, and hanging.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem A GENTLEMAN; opens “"HE has robbed two clubs. The judge at Salisbury Can't give him more than he undoubtedly…”; closes “…all As if he were his own son. I pray God Save him from justice! Nicer man never trod."”.

questions.prompt: What does the stranger say about the thief, and what do the two lines after his speech reveal about the stranger himself?
facilitatorNotes: He calls him a scoundrel and a lady-killer and says hanging is “too good by half.” The poet adds that the stranger has crimes of his own, “yet undiscovered or undone”: those who judge loudest are not innocent, only not found out, or not yet guilty.
evidence: Deserves. The scoundrel! Look at his photograph!
With crimes yet undiscovered or undone.

questions.prompt: Why does the Gipsy woman call the same man a gentleman? What does she value?
facilitatorNotes: He paid toward Carrie’s baby promptly, was never mean, invited her and Joe to call, and put his arms round her Amos “as if he were his own son.” She values generosity, kindness and keeping faith with poor people, which he showed her, rather than honesty toward the rich.
evidence: Had a baby he paid up so readily
For I never knew him mean.

questions.prompt: “I pray God / Save him from justice!” Which judgment does the poem leave stronger? What does the title now mean?
facilitatorNotes: Thomas gives her the last and longest word and lets her prayer stand without comment, after undercutting the stranger. The title turns the word “gentleman” from social rank to conduct. A reader may still find her loyalty blind to his crimes; the poem shows both views but sides with her warmth.
evidence: Save him from justice! Nicer man never trod.
Now he was what I call a gentleman.

readings.title: The Bridge
readings.challenge: Find the rhymes hidden inside the lines, and the pause the whole poem describes.
readings.focus: A traveller at rest between past and future, and the strange happiness of belonging to neither.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Goodlier means better, finer.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE BRIDGE; opens “I HAVE come a long way to-day: On a strange bridge alone, Remembering friends, old…”; closes “…hide what has never been, Things goodlier, lovelier, dearer, than will be or have been.”.

questions.prompt: Where is the speaker, and how does he think of his friends?
facilitatorNotes: Alone on a strange bridge after a long day’s journey, remembering old friends “without smile or moan,” as he imagines they remember him. The feeling is neither joy nor grief but a calm detachment.
evidence: On a strange bridge alone,
As they remember me without smile or moan.

questions.prompt: What does the stream do to the past and the future? Listen also for the rhymes inside the lines (“behind, the kind,” “dream. The stream”).
facilitatorNotes: It “drowns” them: kind and unkind friends are “no more / To-night than a dream,” and the future goes the same way. The inner rhymes slow the lines and make the sound flow like the stream. The poem holds a moment when nothing behind or ahead has any hold.
evidence: Runs softly yet drowns the Past,
The dark-lit stream has drowned the Future and the

questions.prompt: Why is this “moment brief between / Two lives” the most blest rest? What does the dusk hide?
facilitatorNotes: Between the life behind and the life ahead, the traveller owes nothing to either. The falling dark hides “what has never been,” things finer than anything that will be or has been: unlived possibilities. Some readers find the poem peaceful; others hear a wish to escape life altogether. Both readings fit Thomas, a restless walker.
evidence: Than this moment brief between
And shades hide what has never been,

readings.title: Bright Clouds
readings.challenge: Follow a single sentence-like poem across lines of every length, and notice the one comparison that does not belong to the pond.
readings.focus: A still, bright pond where nothing need be done, except for one image of war.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. May is hawthorn blossom, which drops white petals in late spring; a bay is a stretch of water bordered by reeds; a moorhen is a small black water bird; to fret is to ruffle; naught means nothing.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem BRIGHT CLOUDS; opens “BRIGHT clouds of may Shade half the pond. Beyond, All but one bay Of emerald Tall reeds…”; closes “…Till the moorhen calls Again Naught's to be done By birds or men. Still the may falls.”.

questions.prompt: What is moving in the scene, and what is still?
facilitatorNotes: The clouds shade half the pond, the wind ruffles the water and drifts the fallen blossom, and the may keeps falling; the bay of emerald reeds lies still and bright, and “No one heeds.” The very short lines make the eye move slowly across the scene.
evidence: Lies bright as the sun.
No one heeds.

questions.prompt: Why might Thomas compare the reeds to “criss-cross bayonets”? How does the comparison change the scene?
facilitatorNotes: Bayonets are blades on soldiers’ rifles; Thomas, writing in wartime, sees the reeds the way a soldier might. The image brings war into a peaceful pond for one line, then is dropped. Readers may feel the war present everywhere in his mind, even here.
evidence: Like criss-cross bayonets
Where a bird once called,

questions.prompt: “Naught’s to be done / By birds or men.” Is this peaceful, or helpless? How does the last line answer?
facilitatorNotes: Until the moorhen calls, nothing needs doing: a pause of perfect quiet. But a reader who remembers the bayonets may hear the helplessness of men facing what they cannot change. “Still the may falls” keeps both: the blossom goes on falling, beautiful and passing.
evidence: Naught's to be done
Still the may falls.

readings.title: May 23
readings.challenge: Enjoy a portrait of a country character, then reread it in the light of the last line.
readings.focus: A perfect spring day, a free gift of flowers, and a man who vanishes.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Thomas lived for some years in the village of Steep in Hampshire; Oakshott and Wheatham Hill are places near it. Cowslips are yellow spring wildflowers; cress is watercress, which grows in clear streams, and a rill is a small stream; flints are stones in the road; a bur is a prickly seed-head that clings to clothes; a copse is a small wood; midges are tiny biting flies.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem MAY 23; opens “THERE never was a finer day, And never will be while May is May,-- The third, and not the…”; closes “…the road like hops, That fine day, May the twenty-third, The day Jack Noman disappeared.”.

questions.prompt: Who is Jack Noman, and how does the speaker feel about him? Find details that show both his roughness and his charm.
facilitatorNotes: He is old, crooked and “jaunty,” perhaps a little drunk (“Who could say if his roll / Came from . . . ale?”), with leaves and burs on his coat from sleeping outdoors. He is brown as the ploughland and wears cowslips in his button-hole and cap. The speaker likes him without reservation: he is “welcome as the nightingale.”
evidence: He was welcome as the nightingale.
That clung to his coat from last night's bed,

questions.prompt: “Where did they come from, Jack?” “Don't ask it, / And you'll be told no lies.” What does this exchange suggest? Why does Jack refuse to sell?
facilitatorNotes: Jack hints that the cresses and cowslips were gathered where he had no right to them, and the speaker answers that in that case he can’t buy. Jack gives them away instead, with a hint that “something” in return next time would be welcome. Both play a game of manners that keeps the gift honest and the friendship easy.
evidence: And you'll be told no lies.
Take them and these flowers, too, free.

questions.prompt: The poem opens with a perfect day and ends “The day Jack Noman disappeared.” How does the last line change what came before? Why might Thomas call him “Noman”?
facilitatorNotes: The whole poem turns out to be the memory of a last meeting; the speaker’s gladness and the fear in the first stanza that the fine weather “could not last” take on new weight. “Noman” sounds like “no man” or nobody: a wanderer without a fixed place, who can vanish without anyone knowing where. Readers may feel the poem itself is the only record he leaves.
evidence: The day Jack Noman disappeared.
And the morrow with fear that it could not last

readings.title: The Green Roads
readings.challenge: Listen to the word that ends the first line of every couplet, and to the rhymes hidden inside the second lines.
readings.focus: The edge of a forest, where people and memories go and do not return.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Green roads are grassy tracks; a castle keep is the strongest central tower of a castle; to twiddle is to play idly with something.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE GREEN ROADS; opens “THE green roads that end in the forest Are strewn with white goose feathers this June,”; closes “…feathers at the edge of the forest, And hear all day long the thrush repeat his song.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker see and hear at the edge of the forest? Sort the details into what stays and what goes.
facilitatorNotes: Goose feathers like a track left by someone who “has never come back”; cottages; an old man and a child wandering towards the trees; a thrush singing; young trees and one dead oak. The cottages and the song stay; the traveller, the old man and the child go, or drift towards going.
evidence: To show his track. But he has never come back.
An old man along the green road to the forest

questions.prompt: Every couplet’s first line ends with “forest.” What is the effect of that repetition, and of the rhymes inside the second lines?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition pulls every line back to the forest, like a refrain or like the thrush that repeats its song. The internal rhymes (back/track, towers/flowers, one/alone, long/song) make the second lines chime and turn back on themselves. Readers may find the sound soothing, or hypnotic and slightly ominous.
evidence: Round one the nettle towers; two are bathed in flowers.
All day long a thrush twiddles his song.

questions.prompt: “All things forget the forest / Excepting perhaps me.” Why is the speaker the one who remembers? What might the forest stand for in a poem by a man who died in the war soon after writing it?
facilitatorNotes: The oak saw “the ages pass,” but it is dead and its memories are lost; only the speaker holds the scene in mind. The forest can be read as the past, as death, or as the unknown into which people vanish, like the traveller who never came back. The poem never says, and its plain, quiet details leave the reader to feel it.
evidence: For the tree is dead: all things forget the forest
Excepting perhaps me, when now I see

readings.title: The Mill-Pond
readings.challenge: Mark where the storm is coming and where it breaks, and how a memory of a girl is bound up with it.
readings.focus: A warning ignored and resented, then understood, years later, as kindness.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A mill-pond holds water for a water mill, which pours through a sluice in a plunge; a wagtail is a small bird that flicks its tail; alders and aspens are waterside trees; starlings are noisy, chattering birds.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE MILL-POND; opens “THE sun blazed while the thunder yet Added a boom: A wagtail flickered bright over The…”; closes “…and as I crouched To shelter, how Beautiful and kind, too, she seemed, As she does now!”.

questions.prompt: How is the coming storm described in the first three stanzas? What is strange about the sounds?
facilitatorNotes: The sun still blazes while thunder booms; a wagtail flickers over the dark pond; the thunder sounds quieter than the doves cooing and the water plunging, and scared starlings out-chatter both the stream and the next roar. The danger is close but drowned out by ordinary noises.
evidence: Less than the cooing in the alder
Sounded the thunder through that plunge

questions.prompt: What did the girl say, and how did the speaker feel about it then?
facilitatorNotes: Seeing him dangle his feet over the foam, she said “Take care!”; she startled him, standing close and dressed in white, and he was angry until she had gone. A boy’s pride resents being warned, especially by a girl.
evidence: A girl came out. "Take care!" she said--
Ages ago I was angry till

questions.prompt: How does the storm change his view of her? Why might the poem end in the present tense, “As she does now”?
facilitatorNotes: When the storm burst and he crouched for shelter, she seemed “beautiful and kind”; her warning had been right. “Ages ago,” repeated, shows how far back this is, yet she still seems so now. Memory keeps her kindness, and perhaps the speaker, a grown man, still wishes for such warnings.
evidence: Then the storm burst, and as I crouched
As she does now!

readings.title: Tall Nettles
readings.challenge: Look at what the nettles cover and what the speaker chooses to love, and ask what the last line adds.
readings.focus: A neglected farmyard corner and a poet’s preference for the overlooked.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Nettles are stinging weeds that grow on disturbed, rich ground. A harrow is a toothed frame dragged over ploughed land; a stone roller flattens it; an elm butt is the stump or thick base of an elm.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem TALL NETTLES; opens “TALL nettles cover up, as they have done These many springs, the rusty harrow, the plough…”; closes “…I like the dust on the nettles, never lost Except to prove the sweetness of a shower.”.

questions.prompt: What lies under the nettles? What does this tell you about the farm?
facilitatorNotes: A rusty harrow, a worn-out plough and a stone roller, old tools abandoned “these many springs”; only an elm stump rises above the weeds. The farm has moved on, or declined, and nature has quietly taken the corner back.
evidence: These many springs, the rusty harrow, the plough
Only the elm butt tops the nettles now.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker like this corner “most”? What does he like about the nettles?
facilitatorNotes: He likes the dust on the nettles as well as any bloom on a flower: the dull, unlovely thing as much as the pretty one. The choice is quietly against conventional ideas of beauty. Ask whether he likes the corner because it is neglected.
evidence: This corner of the farmyard I like most:
As well as any bloom upon a flower

questions.prompt: The dust is “never lost / Except to prove the sweetness of a shower.” What does this last line mean?
facilitatorNotes: Rain washes the dust off, and only then does one feel how sweet the shower is: the dust is there to make the rain welcome. The poem values ordinary dryness and decay because they make refreshment felt. Some readers hear a wartime meaning too: plainness and endurance, then relief.
evidence: Except to prove the sweetness of a shower.
I like the dust on the nettles, never lost

readings.title: Haymaking
readings.challenge: Watch the poem move from a lively morning to a scene where everything stops, and ask what the stillness is for.
readings.focus: An English hayfield at rest, turned by the poem into a picture outside time.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. John Clare was a poet of country life, William Cobbett a writer on rural England, and George Morland and John Crome painters of farms and landscapes, all from around 1800. Holly sheds old leaves in early summer; the mill-foot is where water leaves a mill; the nettle-creeper is a country name for the whitethroat, a small warbler; a tosser is a machine for turning hay to dry it; the team is the waggon’s horses; woodbine is honeysuckle; a grange is a farmhouse with its barns.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem HAYMAKING; opens “AFTER night's thunder far away had rolled The fiery day had a kernel sweet of cold, And…”; closes “…All of us gone out of the reach of change-- Immortal in a picture of an old grange.”.

questions.prompt: The poem begins after a night of thunder. Which details make the morning seem new, almost the first morning of the world?
facilitatorNotes: The clouds uncurl “Like the first gods before they made the world / And misery”; the mill water tumbles “happier than any crowd” of children let out of school; the birds sing “unceasingly” and the swift shrieks in “fierce glee.” Everything is fresh, joyful and before sorrow.
evidence: Like the first gods before they made the world
Of children pouring out of school aloud.

questions.prompt: Halfway through, the poem stops moving. List what is still, and say how the sentences and rhythm change.
facilitatorNotes: The haymakers rest, the tosser lies “forsook,” the waggon stands without its team, the horses wait in the shade, and the men lean on their rakes “about to begin, / But still.” Short sentences and the repeated “still” and “silent” slow the verse as the scene holds its breath.
evidence: The men leaned on their rakes, about to begin,
But still. And all were silent. All was old,

questions.prompt: The scene is “Older than Clare and Cobbett, Morland and Crome” and ends as “a picture of an old grange.” What does it mean for the haymakers to be “out of the reach of change,” and why might a poet in wartime want that?
facilitatorNotes: The moment becomes timeless, like a painting or a country poem: the men, horses and tools say what they will say for ever. Yet the line also says “All of us gone,” so timelessness comes at the cost of being past. Written during the war, the poem can be read as preserving an England that soldiers fought for, or as an elegy for a life about to vanish; both readings fit.
evidence: All of us gone out of the reach of change--
Immortal in a picture of an old grange.

readings.title: Gone, Gone Again
readings.challenge: Follow a poem that slides from the passing seasons to the war and then to a dark, empty house.
readings.focus: Time, loss and a speaker who compares himself to an abandoned house.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Blenheim oranges are a variety of apple, ripe in late summer; quays are wharves where ships load and unload; dung is manure; outmoded means old-fashioned; untenanted means with no one living in it.
readings.contentNote: Speaks bluntly of young men killed in the war.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem GONE, GONE AGAIN; opens “GONE, gone again, May, June, July, And August gone, Again gone by,”; closes “…one pane to reflect the sun, For the schoolboys to throw at-- They have broken every one.”.

questions.prompt: Why were the summer months “Not memorable / Save that I saw them go”? What does the image of rivers flowing past empty quays add?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing happened in them worth remembering except their passing. The river keeps moving past quays where no ships load: motion with nothing carried, time going by without use. The short lines make the months go quickly.
evidence: Not memorable
As past the empty quays

questions.prompt: The apples fall now “As when I was young,” when “the lost one was here,” and when the war began. What links the three times, and how does the stanza’s last line change the tone?
facilitatorNotes: The same harvest rain and grubby falling apples recur across his life and mark it like a clock. The last line, “To turn young men to dung,” is brutally plain after the quiet; it echoes the rotting fruit, as if the dead were only another fallen crop. “The lost one” is never named, which makes the loss more private.
evidence: Fall grubby from the trees,
To turn young men to dung.

questions.prompt: “I am something like that.” How is the speaker like the old house, and how is he different? What do the broken panes suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Like the house he is old-fashioned, dignified and empty of “the friendliness, the strife” of life. Unlike it he is “still breathing and interested” in houses that are lit. But he has “Not one pane to reflect the sun”: nothing in him can give back light, and small careless damage (schoolboys’ stones) has done it. Readers may hear depression, war-weariness, or both.
evidence: Still breathing and interested
They have broken every one.

readings.title: The Sun Used to Shine
readings.challenge: Notice how the war enters and leaves a poem about two friends walking, and what the ending does with their memory.
readings.focus: A friendship in the first months of the war, remembered after it has passed.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. The poem remembers walks in Gloucestershire in the late summer of 1914, just after the war began, with the American poet Robert Frost, who encouraged Thomas to write poetry. Betonies are purple wildflowers; Hades is the underworld of Greek myth; the Crusades were medieval religious wars; aught means anything.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE SUN USED TO SHINE; opens “THE sun used to shine while we two walked Slowly together, paused and started Again, and…”; closes “…through other flowers In those fields under the same moon Go talking and have easy hours.”.

questions.prompt: How did the two walkers spend their days? What does the poem say they paid “small heed” to?
facilitatorNotes: They walked, paused, mused or talked “As either pleased,” never disagreed about where to rest, and gave little thought to the future or the recent past. Talk of men, poetry and the war gave way easily to an apple hollowed by wasps or a flower at the forest’s edge. The ease of the friendship shows in the easy rhythm.
evidence: As either pleased, and cheerfully parted
And the late past we gave small heed.

questions.prompt: The war is “remote” here. When does it come back to mind, and how do the friends keep it at a distance?
facilitatorNotes: At moonrise, when they think of soldiers far to the east who see the same moon. Yet they could “as well imagine the Crusades / Or Caesar’s battles”: the war seems as far away as ancient history. The crocuses born “In sunless Hades fields” hint at death even in the flowers.
evidence: Came back to mind with the moonrise
Could as well imagine the Crusades

questions.prompt: From “Everything / To faintness like those rumours fades” the poem piles up similes. What fades, and how does the last stanza answer that loss?
facilitatorNotes: The brook’s glitter, the walks, the two men, the apples, the talks and silences all fade like sand covered by the tide. The last stanza imagines “other men through other flowers” in the same fields under the same moon. That can be consoling, because life and friendship go on, or painful, because the speaker and his walks are replaceable. Readers may add that Thomas himself was killed in the war he once found remote.
evidence: And silences--like memory's sand
Go talking and have easy hours.

readings.title: October
readings.challenge: Compare the earth’s mood with the speaker’s, and decide what the last lines conclude about happiness.
readings.focus: A beautiful autumn day, and a man who cannot be as happy as the day is beautiful.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Thomas suffered from long periods of depression; melancholy is a lasting, heavy sadness. Harebell, scabious and tormentil are small wildflowers of hill pasture; gossamers are fine spider threads that drift in the air; gorse is a prickly shrub that flowers in almost every month of the year.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem OCTOBER; opens “THE green elm with the one great bough of gold Lets leaves into the grass slip, one by…”; closes “…day, And this mood by the name of melancholy Shall no more blackened and obscured be.”.

questions.prompt: Find details in the first stanza that show how gently autumn is arriving.
facilitatorNotes: The elm lets its leaves slip “one by one”; the wind is too light to shake birch leaves off the fern; the gossamers “wander at their own will”; only the squirrels complain, at steps heavier than birds’. Nothing is violent; autumn comes almost as softly as spring.
evidence: Lets leaves into the grass slip, one by one,--
The gossamers wander at their own will.

questions.prompt: The speaker says he “might / As happy be as earth is beautiful, / Were I some other.” What stands between him and happiness?
facilitatorNotes: The earth renews itself season by season, so that October can feel “fresh again and new / As Spring”; he cannot turn with the seasons, and he cannot be someone else. The problem is not the day but the self who sees it, unlike the gorse, which has “no time not to be gay.”
evidence: As happy be as earth is beautiful,
Were I some other or with earth could turn

questions.prompt: How do the last four lines change the speaker’s judgment of the day? Is the ending hopeful?
facilitatorNotes: He wonders whether this is happiness after all, and predicts that one day he will remember it as a happy day and stop calling his mood melancholy. Happiness, it seems, may be recognized only in memory. Some readers find that consoling; others find it sad that joy can be known only afterwards; the “who knows?” keeps both open.
evidence: But if this be not happiness,--who knows?
Some day I shall think this a happy day,

readings.title: The Long Small Room
readings.challenge: Follow the poem from a room to its silent witnesses to the speaker’s own writing hand.
readings.focus: A room remembered, things that happened there which no one could prevent, and a writer moving toward age.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A casement is a window hinged at the side; ivy grows thick round old brick walls. Willows lose their long narrow leaves late in autumn.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE LONG SMALL ROOM; opens “THE long small room that showed willows in the west Narrowed up to the end the fireplace…”; closes “…more starting to crawl on towards age. The hundred last leaves stream upon the willow.”.

questions.prompt: What is the room like, and what puzzles the speaker about it?
facilitatorNotes: Long and narrow, with willows seen to the west and a fireplace filling the narrow end; he liked it, and no one knew “what need or accident” made the builders shape it so. The opening is calm, almost fond.
evidence: I liked it. No one guessed
What need or accident made them so build.

questions.prompt: Who are the only witnesses to what happened in the room? Why does the speaker compare himself to them?
facilitatorNotes: The moon, a mouse and a sparrow peeping through the ivy; they will keep the tale “for the old ivy and older brick.” Looking back, he is like them: he saw what he “could never understand / Or alter or prevent.” The poem hints at something painful in “the dark house” without saying what.
evidence: When I look back I am like moon, sparrow and mouse
That witnessed what they could never understand

questions.prompt: What “remains the same”? How does the image of the hand change the poem’s mood?
facilitatorNotes: His right hand, crawling “crab-like” across the clean page each morning, resting, then crawling on “towards age”: the writer’s daily labour. The crab image is awkward and slow, not heroic. The last line, leaves streaming from the willow, ends with autumn and loss.
evidence: Crawling crab-like over the clean white page,
The hundred last leaves stream upon the willow.

readings.title: Liberty
readings.challenge: Follow the speaker’s argument about freedom, and notice where it turns.
readings.focus: Being free to do anything and wanting nothing, and a choice, at the end, for imperfect life.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Thomas often wrote about his long spells of depression and his difficulty in deciding how to live. “Half in love” echoes John Keats’s “Ode to a Nightingale,” in which Keats says he has been “half in love with easeful Death.”
readings.contentNote: Explores depression and a wish to wipe out one’s own past, which the poem turns away from at the end.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem LIBERTY; opens “THE last light has gone out of the world, except This moonlight lying on the grass like…”; closes “…that have an end, with life and earth, And this moon that leaves me dark within the door.”.

questions.prompt: Describe the scene. What has the moonlight done to the world, and why does the speaker feel that he and the moon alone are left?
facilitatorNotes: The last light is gone and moonlight lies “like frost” beyond the elm’s shadow. It seems everything else has slept for ages, the past and even his own thoughts buried, while he and the moon “stand idle over the grave.” The scene makes him a survivor with nothing to do.
evidence: This moonlight lying on the grass like frost
Live yet and here stand idle over the grave

questions.prompt: “There's none less free than who / Does nothing and has nothing else to do.” Explain the paradox. What kind of liberty does the speaker have?
facilitatorNotes: Freedom with nothing one wants to do is no freedom at all: he is free “only for what is not to his mind,” and nothing is to his mind. He and the moon have liberty only “To dream what we could do if we were free.” Liberty without desire feels like emptiness.
evidence: There's none less free than who
Being free only for what is not to his mind,

questions.prompt: Keats was “half in love with easeful Death”; Thomas is “half in love with pain.” What does he choose instead of wiping out his hours, and how does the final image leave him?
facilitatorNotes: He turns from the wish to erase his past toward “what is imperfect,” tears and mirth, “things that have an end, with life and earth.” Choosing pain and imperfection over death is a choice for living. But the moon “leaves me dark within the door”: he stands on a threshold, still in shadow. Readers can argue whether the ending affirms life or only just holds on to it.
evidence: And yet I still am half in love with pain,
And this moon that leaves me dark within the door.

readings.title: November
readings.challenge: Look closely at what most people would call ugly, and compare two ways of looking up from it.
readings.focus: Mud and clean sky: a defence of the dirty earth.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. This is one of the first poems he wrote, at the end of 1914. Hobnails are short nails in the soles of heavy boots; “charactered” means written, like the letters of an alphabet; dinted means dented.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem NOVEMBER; opens “NOVEMBER'S days are thirty: November's earth is dirty, Those thirty days, from first to…”; closes “…is to the sky; He loves even the mud whose dyes Renounce all brightness to the skies.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the paths “the prettiest things on ground” in a month whose earth is “dirty”?
facilitatorNotes: They are printed with the marks of boots and of small animals and birds, “foot and wing-tip overprinted / Or separately charactered,” like writing. The mud keeps a record of every life that crossed it, which makes it beautiful to a careful eye.
evidence: With foot and wing-tip overprinted
Of little beast and little bird.

questions.prompt: Find the list of what makes up the mud. Why does the poet bother to name what “men scorn”?
facilitatorNotes: “Twig, leaf, flint, thorn, / Straw, feather”: short, packed lines that mash things together as the mud does. By naming each thing he refuses to dismiss it with one word; the abrupt “Condemned as mud” sounds like an unfair verdict.
evidence: Twig, leaf, flint, thorn,
Condemned as mud.

questions.prompt: Two people stare up at the clean November sky. How do they differ, and which does the poem seem to prefer?
facilitatorNotes: One imagines a refuge in the pure sky, away from the mud. The other loves earth and November more, because without them the sky would mean as little to him as he does to the sky; he loves even the mud for giving all its brightness to the heavens. The poem ends with the second, which suggests its sympathy, though readers may see the two as moods any one person might have.
evidence: One imagines a refuge there
He loves even the mud whose dyes

readings.title: The Sheiling
readings.challenge: Trace how the poem moves from the stony land to the inside of the house and back out again.
readings.focus: A house so at peace with its wild setting that the cold stone itself seems kind.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A sheiling (shieling) is a hut or small house on high, rough grazing land in the North of England or Scotland, first used by herdsmen in summer.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE SHEILING; opens “IT stands alone Up in a land of stone All worn like ancient stairs, A land of rocks and…”; closes “…land that gave it peace, And the stone has taken the house To its cold heart and is kind.”.

questions.prompt: What kind of land does the house stand in?
facilitatorNotes: A land of stone and rock, worn “like ancient stairs,” with trees “nourished on wind and stone.” It is harsh and old, and the house stands alone in it.
evidence: Up in a land of stone
All worn like ancient stairs,

questions.prompt: What has made the inside of the house what it is? What do people inside hear and see?
facilitatorNotes: “Arts and kindliness” over many years have coloured, sweetened and warmed it. Safe within, people hear the wind as music and see the same wild land as pictures. The house turns harshness into art without shutting it out.
evidence: By arts and kindliness
But music, pictures see

questions.prompt: “One maker’s mind / Made both.” What is the relation between house and land in the last stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Both seem made by one mind, so they belong together: the house is kind to the land that gave it peace, and the stone has taken the house “to its cold heart and is kind.” The cold landscape becomes kind. Ask whether the poem praises the people of the house, the place, or the harmony between them.
evidence: One maker's mind
To its cold heart and is kind.

readings.title: The Gallows
readings.challenge: Listen to the ballad’s refrains, and ask what the poem might be about besides a gamekeeper’s gibbet.
readings.focus: A nursery-rhyme tune for the bodies of shot animals.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Gamekeepers protected the pheasants on country estates by killing animals that preyed on them or their eggs, and often hung the bodies in a row on a fence or tree, a “gamekeeper’s gallows,” to show their employer and to warn other animals. A keeper here is a gamekeeper.
readings.contentNote: Describes animals shot and their bodies left hanging.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE GALLOWS; opens “THERE was a weasel lived in the sun With all his family, Till a keeper shot him with his…”; closes “…In the sun and in the snow, Without pain, without pleasure, On the dead oak tree bough.”.

questions.prompt: What does the poem say about each animal’s life, and what happens to every one?
facilitatorNotes: The weasel lived “in the sun / With all his family”; the crow was “a thief and a murderer”; the magpie could “both talk and do.” Whatever their lives, innocent or guilty, clever or not, the keeper shoots them all and hangs them on the same bough.
evidence: a weasel lived in the sun
But a thief and a murderer

questions.prompt: Which lines return, with small changes, in every stanza? What do the refrains and the jingling rhythm do to the subject?
facilitatorNotes: “In the sun and in the snow,” “Without pleasure, without pain” and “On the dead oak tree bough,” reversed in the last stanza to “Without pain, without pleasure.” The nursery-rhyme beat makes the deaths sound like a children’s song, which is both gentle and chilling; the refrains swing like the bodies, for ever.
evidence: Without pleasure, without pain,
Without pain, without pleasure,

questions.prompt: “There are no more sins to be sinned,” and the dead have “endless leisure.” Is the poem only about vermin on a gibbet? Consider that Thomas wrote it during the First World War.
facilitatorNotes: The irony is plain: death ends sin and gives leisure no one wanted, and the magpie’s talents did not “avail.” Many readers hear the war’s dead in “many other beasts / And birds . . . / taken from their feasts / And hung up there together”; others read it as a clear-eyed country poem about killing in the name of game. The poem never says, so both readings rest on the same details.
evidence: There are no more sins to be sinned
To swing and have endless leisure

readings.title: Birds’ Nests
readings.challenge: Notice how the speaker treats a small embarrassment, and where the poem turns from shame to pleasure.
readings.focus: Seeing what was there all along, and the second life of empty nests.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A dormouse is a small, nut-eating animal like a mouse; goose-grass is a sticky climbing weed; jays are birds of the crow family that rob other birds’ nests; “no game” means no challenge.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem BIRDS’ NESTS; opens “THE summer nests uncovered by autumn wind. Some torn, others dislodged, all dark.…”; closes “…dormouse dined there on hazel-nuts, And grass and goose-grass seeds found soil and grew.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker feel “a little shame” when the autumn wind uncovers the nests?
facilitatorNotes: He missed most of them all summer, even nests at eye level, and now anyone can see them. Finding nests used to be a skill, almost a game; now the bare branches make it “no game.” The shame is a countryman’s, proud of how closely he looks.
evidence: I cannot help a little shame
The leaves blew off and made the seeing no game.

questions.prompt: “'Tis a light pang.” What pleasure does he set against it?
facilitatorNotes: The pleasure of seeing the nests “in their places, now first known,” near home and on distant roads, and of knowing that their secret was kept all summer from boys (if not from jays and squirrels). The nests show how much went on unseen.
evidence: Still in their places, now first known,
Boys knew them not,

questions.prompt: The poem ends with the winter nests that leaves and berries fell into. What has happened to them, and what might this say about things that are hidden or finished?
facilitatorNotes: A dormouse ate its hazel-nuts there, and seeds found soil and grew: the empty nest has become a tiny garden. Something finished with its first purpose shelters new life. Readers may connect this with memory, with hidden lives, or simply with the value of looking closely; the poem does not insist.
evidence: Once a dormouse dined there on hazel-nuts,
And grass and goose-grass seeds found soil and grew.

readings.title: “Home”
readings.challenge: Notice what the three walkers share and what they keep to themselves, and why the speaker stops at a single word.
readings.focus: Comrades who are not friends, a word that cannot be said, and homesickness kept under control.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. From 1915 he was a soldier, and in 1916 he was teaching at an army camp in Essex; this poem is usually read as a walk back to camp with two fellow soldiers after a day out in the snow. A league is about three miles; the three men come from three counties far apart.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “HOME”; opens “FAIR was the morning, fair our tempers, and We had seen nothing fairer than that land,…”; closes “…else I should be Another man, as often now I seem, Or this life be only an evil dream.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the three walk faster when they see “the cold roofs”? What is waiting for them there?
facilitatorNotes: There is “nothing to return for, except need”: food, sleep and the company of men they have lived with. They have never been happy there and could not be. Someone’s joke about the “beaten horse” running home puts their eagerness in its place.
evidence: There was nothing to return for, except need,
Happy we had not been there, nor could be.

questions.prompt: The word “home” raises a smile in all three. What does the smile mean, and why does no one say so?
facilitatorNotes: The camp is not home; each is thinking of his own home far away. The smile admits it without words, and saying more would break the rule of the place: they are “fellows in a union that ends / With the necessity for it,” not friends. Readers may find this honest about wartime comradeship, or bleak.
evidence: That all knew what he meant and none would say.
But fellows in a union that ends

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker allow himself only “the mere word” “Homesick”? What does he fear would happen if he admitted more?
facilitatorNotes: If he let the feeling in fully he “could not endure it / For a day longer”: he would become “Another man,” or his life would seem “an evil dream.” Keeping the word playful is how he survives the “captivity.” Yet the poem itself admits more than the word, which shows what the restraint costs.
evidence: If I should ever more admit
Or this life be only an evil dream.

readings.title: There’s Nothing Like the Sun
readings.challenge: Notice where the poem stops describing November and starts arguing with itself.
readings.focus: Praise of the late-year sun that widens to every month, and closes on death.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. Damsons are small, dark purple plums; spangles are glittering drops. Starlings are mimics: this one whistles “what / Once swallows sang,” imitating birds that have left for the winter.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THERE’S NOTHING LIKE THE SUN; opens “THERE'S nothing like the sun as the year dies, Kind as it can be, this world being made…”; closes “…nothing like the sun that shines to-day" There's nothing like the sun till we are dead.”.

questions.prompt: What does the November sun do in the first part of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It is kind to everything it touches except snow; it warms the south wall where the speaker stands; it lights the damsons falling with raindrops as a starling shakes the bough. The scene is the last richness of the year.
evidence: The south wall warms me: November has begun,
While the sweet last-left damsons from the bough

questions.prompt: “But I have not forgot.” What does the speaker remember, and how does the list of months change the poem’s claim?
facilitatorNotes: That every month has its own sun: he names them all, as if correcting himself. On any day he has said, or would say, “There’s nothing like the sun that shines to-day.” Praise of one month becomes praise of every day as it comes.
evidence: But I have not forgot
No day of any month but I have said--

questions.prompt: Read the last line twice. What are its two meanings? Why might it matter that a soldier wrote it?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing equals the sun as long as we live; and the sun is the best thing until death ends our seeing it. “If I could live long enough” has already raised the thought. Thomas wrote these poems knowing he might be killed; the cheerful saying ends with a reminder of death.
evidence: There's nothing like the sun till we are dead.
Or, if I could live long enough, should say--

readings.title: An Old Song
readings.challenge: Watch a walker at sunset who keeps singing an old song that seems to say the opposite of what he feels.
readings.focus: A private path of light, and an old sailors’ song that charms the singer.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. “I'll go no more a-roving” is the chorus of an old sailors’ song, a shanty, whose verse Thomas quotes at the end in italics; to rove is to wander, and a rover can also be a man who goes from one woman to another. Elate means in high spirits; a gull’s cry is called mewing.
readings.contentNote: Quotes a bawdy sailors’ song about a woman of Amsterdam; Thomas mentions its “lewdness.”

excerpt.locator: Complete poem AN OLD SONG; opens “THE sun set, the wind fell, the sea Was like a mirror shaking: The one small wave that…”; closes “…a-roving, since roving's been my ruin, I'll go no more a-roving with you, fair maid._”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker see at sunset, and why does he stress that “no one else in the whole world / Saw that same sight”?
facilitatorNotes: A strip of light on the sea like a narrow bright footbridge reaching to him. A path of light on water always points at the person looking, so each viewer sees a different one: the sight is his alone, and as he walks it stays “Just one step from my feet.”
evidence: Like a straight narrow footbridge bright
Saw that same sight.

questions.prompt: Why does he keep repeating “I'll go no more a-roving” while he walks “elate”? Is there a contrast between the words and his mood?
facilitatorNotes: The song is a sailor’s regret (“roving's been my ruin”), but he sings it happily while wandering. He says himself that the “wild charm” of the chorus outweighs its words. The tune and the evening matter more than the story the song tells.
evidence: I walked elate, my bridge always
By the wild charm the chorus played:

questions.prompt: Why might Thomas end with the old song’s own verse, in italics, instead of his own words? What does an old song give him that description could not?
facilitatorNotes: The poem gives way to the voice of sailors long gone, mixed with the dusk and the gulls. An old song is shared and anonymous; it connects his private bridge of light to many earlier singers. Readers may also notice the gap between the song’s coarse story and the beauty he hears in it.
evidence: The sailors' song of merry loving
Mark well what I do say--

readings.title: The Penny Whistle
readings.challenge: Track the black and the white through a winter scene, and think about why the poem ends by praising someone else’s music.
readings.focus: Signs of life in a dark winter wood, and a tune that says more than a poem.
readings.context: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) wrote almost all his poems between the end of 1914 and his death in battle at Arras in April 1917; this volume appeared later that year. A bugle is a small brass horn; ghylls are steep, narrow wooded valleys with streams; charcoal-burners lived in the woods, slowly burning wood into charcoal under covered mounds; a caravan-hut is a hut on wheels; a penny whistle is a cheap tin whistle.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE PENNY WHISTLE; opens “THE new moon hangs like an ivory bugle In the naked frosty blue; And the ghylls of the…”; closes “…and surely playing On a whistle an olden nursery melody, Says far more than I am saying.”.

questions.prompt: Find the black and the white in the poem. How do they work against each other?
facilitatorNotes: Black: the ghylls “blackened anew,” the brooks’ “black hollow voices,” the sooty charcoal-burners. White and bright: the ivory moon, the linen on the line, the letter, the hut that “gleams” like a kingfisher, the first primroses. The bright things stand out sharply against the winter dark.
evidence: The charcoal-burners are black, but their linen
And white the letter the girl is reading

questions.prompt: The brooks roar “Betwixt rage and a moan.” Where does the mood change, and what changes it?
facilitatorNotes: The third stanza turns with “But still”: the caravan-hut gleams, and primroses appear round the old hearths. Human life and the first flowers of spring answer the angry, mournful noise of the brooks.
evidence: Betwixt rage and a moan.
First primroses ask to be seen.

questions.prompt: The boy’s tune “Says far more than I am saying.” What might it say? Why would a poet admit that a penny whistle says more than his poem?
facilitatorNotes: The tune is old, simple and played in hiding, slowly and surely; it may carry what the girl’s letter holds, or the feeling of the whole scene, without explaining it. Thomas’s modesty is also a method: like the whistle, his poem shows details and leaves the meaning unsaid. Some readers notice that the moon is compared to a bugle, an army instrument, against which the child’s nursery tune sounds gentler.
evidence: On a whistle an olden nursery melody,
Says far more than I am saying.
